title: “Evil Mickey Mouse” Invades Japan in a 1934 Japanese Anime Propaganda Film
description:
in Film |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in Film |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before the Japan­ese fell com­plete­ly, one hun­dred per­cent in love with any­thing and every­thing Dis­ney (I mean, seri­ous­ly, they love it), Mick­ey Mouse rep­re­sent­ed some­thing com­plete­ly dif­fer­ent: Pure Amer­i­can impe­ri­al­ist evil.
At least he did in this 1934 ani­mat­ed pro­pa­gan­da car­toon Omochabako series dai san wa: Ehon senkya-hyaku­san­ja-rokunen (Toy­box Series 3: Pic­ture Book 1936) by Komat­suza­wa Hajime. It’s a con­vo­lut­ed title, but pret­ty sim­ple in plot. An island of cute crit­ters (includ­ing one Felix the Cat clone) is attacked from the air by an army of Mick­ey Mous­es (Mick­ey Mice?) rid­ing bats and assist­ed by croc­o­diles and snakes that act like machine guns. The fright­ened crea­tures call on the heroes of Japan­ese sto­ry­books and folk leg­ends to help them, from Momo­taro (“Peach Boy”) and Kin­taro (“Gold­en Boy”) to Issun-boshi (“One Inch Boy”) and Benkei, a war­rior monk, to send Mick­ey pack­ing. The not-so-sub­tle mes­sage: Mick­ey Mouse may be your hero, Amer­i­ca, but our char­ac­ters are old­er, more numer­ous, and way more beloved. Our pop cul­ture is old­er than yours!
Though made in 1934, it is set in 1936, which might tie (accord­ing to this site) into the expi­ra­tion of a naval treaty between the Unit­ed States and Japan on that date. The Japan­ese attack on Pearl Har­bor was a full sev­en years off, but clear­ly ten­sions were run­ning high even then, as both the West and Japan had their eyes on Asia and the South Pacif­ic.
Also of note is the trope of char­ac­ters com­ing alive from a sto­ry­book, as this was a favorite sub­ject in sev­er­al Warn­er Bros. car­toons that would come out a few years lat­er (and which we’ve cov­ered).
And final­ly to clar­i­fy Mickey’s fate at the end of the film: the old man with the box is a Rip Van Win­kle char­ac­ter, and in Japan­ese folk­lore he is made old by the con­tents of a box he’s been told not to open. Vio­lence is not van­quished with vio­lence at the end of this car­toon, but with mag­ic and deri­sive laugh­ter fol­lowed by a song. In the real world, things would not end so eas­i­ly.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

title: Route 66 Turns 100 This Year: Take a Tour of America’s Most Famous Highway
description: This past sum­mer, the Unit­ed States of Amer­i­ca cel­e­brat­ed 250 years of inde­pen­dence. But for a great many Amer­i­cana-lovers around
body:
This past sum­mer, the Unit­ed States of Amer­i­ca cel­e­brat­ed 250 years of inde­pen­dence. But for a great many Amer­i­cana-lovers around the world, this year also brings anoth­er, even more res­o­nant date: the 100th anniver­sary of the estab­lish­ment of Route 66. In the months lead­ing up to Novem­ber 11th, the offi­cial birth­day of what John Stein­beck dubbed the “Moth­er Road,” tourists both for­eign and domes­tic have seized the occa­sion to make the 2,448-mile dri­ve of which they’ve long dreamed. Run­ning from Grant Park in Chica­go to the San­ta Mon­i­ca Pier, Route 66 reveals a great swath of Amer­i­ca’s big cities, small towns, his­toric sites, vast open spaces, nat­ur­al won­ders, and — most impor­tant for any enthu­si­ast — pieces of road­side kitsch.
You’ll see plen­ty of all that in the video at the top of the post from Chris Attrell, one of the YouTu­bers who’s marked Route 66’s cen­ten­ni­al year by dri­ving it all and mak­ing a video along the way. He seems to have had less than ide­al luck in reach­ing the attrac­tions on his more than 100 stops dur­ing busi­ness hours, but in the true Amer­i­can spir­it, he express­es opti­mism about get­ting back to them next time.
There are a host of schools of thought on which direc­tion is best to dri­ve the whole of Route 66, but Attrell heads inland from the coast, as trav­el vlog­ger Josh McNair did with his father for his chan­nel Through My Lens a few years before. They take only two weeks to do so, a fair­ly rapid clip at which to cross sev­en states, or eight if you count the tiny seg­ment that pass­es through the south­east cor­ner of Kansas.
httpv:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=H0bA72fjHMQ
There are, no doubt, Route 66 purists who would insist that no stretch, no mat­ter how short, can be bypassed — or at least no stretch of the 85 per­cent of the orig­i­nal high­way that remains dri­vable today. Route 66 was decom­mis­sioned in 1985, near­ly three decades after the con­struc­tion of the U.S. Inter­state High­way Sys­tem began mak­ing it obso­lete. But it was­n’t long there­after that efforts began to pre­serve as much of it as pos­si­ble as His­toric Route 66, an enter­prise that may have ini­tial­ly been dri­ven by nos­tal­gia, but increas­ing­ly trades in the exoti­cism of the once-ordi­nary. It’s easy to over-roman­ti­cize the days of pre-Inter­state auto­mo­bile trav­el, but as the aes­thet­ics and rhythms of life in that peri­od pass out of liv­ing mem­o­ry, their remains become all the more com­pelling, even in total desue­tude.


	

Any­one in search of total desue­tude can hard­ly find more vivid exam­ples, at least in my expe­ri­ence, than the Route 66 ghost towns (and, as Attrell calls them, “semi-ghost towns”) that the free­ways passed by. For exam­ple, the strip of most­ly hol­lowed-out lodg­ings that is Tucum­cari, New Mex­i­co has been a pho­tog­ra­pher’s dream for so long that a non-clichéd shot of the place can now be hard to come by. But for all the books pub­lished about it — and indeed, all the videos made about it — Route 66 is less a sub­ject than an expe­ri­ence, a pil­grim­age through an Amer­i­ca of neon signs, peri­od-accu­rate gas sta­tions, mem­o­ra­bil­ia shops, eccen­tric art­works, hot dogs on sticks, Muf­fler Man stat­ues, din­ers both oper­at­ing and aban­doned, and, of course, wig­wam motels. May it endure to the Unit­ed States’ quin­cen­ten­ni­al.

title: Download Hundreds of Issues of Jugend, Germany’s Pioneering Art Nouveau Magazine (1896–1940)
description: It’s an ungain­ly word for Eng­lish speak­ers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gle­ich­schal­tung. Yet the con­cept remains cen­tral
body:
It’s an ungain­ly word for Eng­lish speak­ers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gle­ich­schal­tung. Yet the con­cept remains cen­tral for a clear view of what hap­pened to Ger­many in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation com­plete­ly trans­formed, seem­ing­ly overnight, through “a con­cert­ed pol­i­cy of ‘coor­di­na­tion’ (Gle­ich­schal­tung),” the U.S. Holo­caust Memo­r­i­al Muse­um writes. “Cul­ture, the econ­o­my, edu­ca­tion, and law all came under Nazi con­trol.” Those artists and orga­ni­za­tions that were not purged had their essen­tial char­ac­ter changed to reflect an entire­ly dif­fer­ent set of artis­tic and polit­i­cal val­ues. One pub­li­ca­tion, espe­cial­ly, serves as an exam­ple of the Naz­i­fi­ca­tion of cul­ture.
The arts jour­nal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned large­ly into pro­pa­gan­da” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But pri­or to the regime’s takeover, Jugend show­cased the most avant-garde, “degen­er­ate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘braini­est’ peri­od­i­cal of the day,” as one crit­ic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Lit­er­ary Mag­a­zine. “There is no mag­a­zine pub­lished in Eng­land or in this coun­try which is at all like it.”
You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and down­load hun­dreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Hei­del­berg’s dig­i­tal archive, thou­sands of pages in PDF form, span­ning the mag­a­zine’s forty-four-year his­to­ry. You can also see images at Flickr.

As in Eng­land, France, Aus­tria, and the U.S., the Art Nou­veau move­ment in Ger­many emerged from a whirl­wind of post-Impres­sion­ist paint­ing, Ori­en­tal­ist motifs, folk art, mod­ernist art and adver­tis­ing, book illus­tra­tion, and graph­ic and indus­tri­al design. Appro­pri­ate­ly, giv­en its perch on the thresh­old of a new cen­tu­ry, Art Nou­veau looked both backward—to the medieval, goth­ic, and Romantic—and for­ward toward a more mod­ernist, urbane, and urban­ized sen­si­bil­i­ty.

So influ­en­tial was Jugend that Art Nou­veau in Ger­many became known as Jugend­stil. The Oxford Crit­i­cal and Cul­tur­al His­to­ry of Mod­ernist Mag­a­zines writes, “Among Jugend’s most impor­tant qualities—indeed, an essen­tial aspect of Art Nou­veau and its Ger­man equiv­a­lent Jugend­stil—was its bril­liant escapism.” Found­ed in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the mag­a­zine was “from the start a venue to pro­mote the new cul­tur­al Renais­sance with­out recourse to the estab­lished ‘vin­tage’ art.” (See its very first cov­er right above.)

Jugend­stil was pri­mar­i­ly based in Munich, where most of its artists, design­ers, and writ­ers lived and worked, until the turn of the cen­tu­ry, when, notes the Art Ency­clo­pe­dia, “the Munich group dis­persed, head­ing for Berlin, Weimar and Darm­stadt.” Art Nou­veau in Ger­many devel­oped in two phas­es, “a pre-1900 phase dom­i­nat­ed by flo­ral motifs, them­selves root­ed in Eng­lish Art Nou­veau and Japan­ese art,” and a “post-1900 phase, marked by a ten­den­cy towards abstract art.”

While we know the names of many Art Nou­veau artists from else­where in Europe—Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec in France, Aubrey Beard­s­ley in Eng­land, Gus­tav Klimt in Aus­tria, for exam­ple—Jugend­stil in Ger­many pro­duced few inter­na­tion­al stars. Many of the artists pub­lished in its pages were rel­a­tive­ly unknown at first. But its shock­ing­ly bril­liant cov­ers and rad­i­cal edi­to­r­i­al tone put it at the fore­front of Ger­man arts for decades. “Jugend’s polit­i­cal and social plat­form,” wrote The Yale Lit­er­ary Mag­a­zine crit­ic, “is one of opposition—opposition to every­thing.”

In 1933, how­ev­er, the mag­a­zine was forced to com­ply with the kind of dour con­ser­vatism it had arisen explic­it­ly to protest. Its wild cov­ers and proud­ly orig­i­nal con­tents turned somber and neo­clas­si­cal, as in the bust of Niet­zsche on the cov­er above from 1934. Many of its artists dis­ap­peared or went into exile. But as we observe this trans­for­ma­tion hap­pen­ing abrupt­ly in the Uni­ver­si­ty of Hei­del­berg archive, we still see a mag­a­zine whose edi­to­r­i­al staff held fast to notions of artis­tic qual­i­ty, as they were forced to turn away from every­thing that had made Jugend excit­ing, cut­ting-edge, and wor­thy of its title.

via Messy Nessy Chic

title: The Ancient Greek Water Clock That Kept the Most Accurate Time for 1,800 Years
description:
in History, Technology |   	September 9th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Today, we’re sur­round­ed by tech­nolo­gies we could jus­ti­fi­ably descr
body:
in History, Technology |   	September 9th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Today, we’re sur­round­ed by tech­nolo­gies we could jus­ti­fi­ably describe as time thieves. In ancient Greece, those who want­ed to know where their time was going con­sult­ed a device they called a “water thief.” The roots of the clep­sy­dra, or water clock, go back as far as the six­teenth cen­tu­ry BC, with evi­dence of such devices found in mod­ern-day Iraq, Iran, and Egypt, and more ambigu­ous evi­dence unearthed in places like India and Chi­na. The mech­a­nism in the ear­li­est exam­ples takes not much more com­plex a form than a bowl out of which water slow­ly drips, albeit not at a reg­u­lar pace. That nat­ur­al imped­i­ment to hydraulic time­keep­ing was­n’t cor­rect­ed until the third cen­tu­ry BC, when a Greek inven­tor called Cte­si­bius set about mak­ing his own improve­ments.
Cte­si­bius’ auto­mat­ic water clock used a ver­ti­cal cylin­der, rotat­ing once year­ly, marked with straight ver­ti­cal lines rep­re­sent­ing the months of the year and curved hor­i­zon­tal lines rep­re­sent­ing the hours of the day. A point­er next to it indi­cat­ed the cur­rent hour, its posi­tion changed by the water lev­el of the cylin­der in which it float­ed. That cylin­der was filled through a feed­ing reser­voir, itself con­stant­ly sup­plied with water.
The idea behind this arrange­ment was to keep the rate of flow steady, and thus the speed of the point­er con­stant. To emp­ty the reser­voir with­out the need for human inter­ven­tion, Cte­si­bius incor­po­rat­ed a siphon that let water out every 24 hours, reset­ting the clock­’s dai­ly cycle. A water wheel attached to a sim­ple sys­tem of gears kept the cylin­der turn­ing, so that its “dis­play” could keep up with the ever-chang­ing length of the day­light-based ancient Greek hour.
All this is explained with detailed visu­al aids in the ani­mat­ed Decon­struct­ed video above. “In a world with­out elec­tric­i­ty, dig­i­tal log­ic, or even mechan­i­cal clocks,” says its nar­ra­tor, “this ancient inven­tion laid the foun­da­tion for automa­tion and time­keep­ing as we know them today.” Indeed, Cte­si­bius’ clep­sy­dra “kept bet­ter time than any­thing else on Earth for 1800 years,” until Chris­ti­aan Huy­gens invent­ed the pen­du­lum clock in 1656. There’s some­thing in the swing­ing of such a mech­a­nism that appeals to the innate human attrac­tion to rhythm, and the metaphor­i­cal val­ue of the grains of sand pass­ing through an hour­glass (an inter­me­di­ary inven­tion between Cte­si­bius and Huy­gens) remains strong even now. But it’s prob­a­bly not a coin­ci­dence that the flow of time and the flow of water, at least from the human per­spec­tive, feel like two aspects of the same pri­mal phe­nom­e­non.

title: Hannah Beuchler Loops Thousands of Colorful Loom Bands like Brushstrokes
description: A decade ago or so, parents were finding loom bands in the couch cushions and underfoot during a craze for the analog toys. Kids made bracelets an
body:
A decade ago or so, parents were finding loom bands in the couch cushions and underfoot during a craze for the analog toys. Kids made bracelets and other items, and in the vein of LEGO and other build-your-own entertainment, YouTube creators provided tutorials for elaborate projects. The toy fad may have waned, but for artist Hannah Beuchler, the small, colorful rubber bands proved an accessible material for an inventive application.
At a glance, Beuchler’s works appear like expressionist paintings, with gestural brushstrokes and carefully chosen colors. But our senses are piqued by the unusual texture, and upon closer inspection, we observe thousands of loom bands in vibrant relief.
Loom band detail
Beuchler draws upon her interest in fabrics and mark-making techniques of the Impressionists. She’s interested in pushing the boundaries of textiles by using found and recycled materials, and her works often plumb the relationship between natural and synthetic media.
Utilizing a felt template, which also serves as the substrate, Beuchler loops the bands onto small tufts of colorful wool roving. Soft and malleable, these segments can be curved and nestled in among one another to create any shape, assembled almost like a puzzle. The finished work retains its textile-like pliability, but when framed and installed on the wall, it assumes the character of a painting.
See more on Beuchler’s work on Instagram.

title: Could a Kid Do It? The Wa Transforms Buildings into Childlike Drawings
description: Although there’s no official count, the amount of World War II bunkers, battery platforms, defensive bollards, and other structures found along Eu
body:
Although there’s no official count, the amount of World War II bunkers, battery platforms, defensive bollards, and other structures found along European coastlines probably number in the tens of thousands. Bunkers were typically made of concrete, and several thousand are located along what’s known as the Atlantic Wall, an extensive coastal network of defenses built by the Nazis between 1942 and 1944 in anticipation of attacks by Allied forces. Disused now for decades, they’re a blight on the landscape, but one that The Wa sees as a blank canvas for something much more playful and bright.
In his series A Kid Could Do It, The Wa transforms otherwise nondescript structures into jubilantly youthful drawings, literally scribbling in saturated colors and adding blocky windows, doors, and flowers. The title of the project, of course, will sound familiar to any artist working in abstraction or museum-goer who has stood looking at a Jackson Pollock or Franz Kline painting and heard someone nearby murmur derisively, “My kid could do that.”

The Wa turns the table on this sentiment, including in a large-scale rendition on an empty house in Stuttgart as part of this year’s PFFFestival. We encounter windows with purple curtains in seemingly random places, a door that’s narrower on the bottom than the top, a roof with scalloped shapes that could be shingles or clouds, and of course, huge scrawls of bright blue and red.
For PFFFestival, as with his earlier bunker paintings, the artist follows what he describes as “one simple rule: the unfiltered creative logic of a child.” A Kid Could Do It also nods to the collaborative nature of how the project began, as The Wa started the series by working alongside his mother. In a manner of speaking, a kid really did do it.
See more on The Wa’s Instagram.






PFFFestival 2026, Stuttgart. Photo by Sven Weber

title: Karla Wong's Folkloric Portraits Conjure Mysterious Portals to Another World
description: Although Karla Wong has always been passionate about drawing, it was her degree in law that ultimately spurred her current practice. The Mexican a
body:
Although Karla Wong has always been passionate about drawing, it was her degree in law that ultimately spurred her current practice. The Mexican artist spent her adolescent and early adult years in Oaxaca, where she attended university and eventually became a forensic and witness sketch artist for the local justice department. Rendering a figure’s likeness based solely on a description is a deeply imaginative process and one that continues to inform the artist’s practice today.
In Journeys of Being on view now at Chicago’s Intuit Art Museum, Wong presents a vibrant body of work that entwines her Oaxacan roots with her Chinese heritage and experiences as a trans woman living between the U.S. and Mexico. Included are vibrant portraits with skeletal figures evocative of Day of the Dead, the folk art sculptures known as alebrijes, and a desert landscape pocked with agave. Victorian garb and faces adorned with makeup gesture toward the performance of gender, too, and the ways we signify beauty and self-expression.
“The Chineses from Laollaga, Oaxaca (Las chinas de Laollaga)” (2024), oil on canvas, 36 x 48 inches
Surrealism and the uncanny inspire much of Wong’s work, and mysterious pockets of clouds and small openings also appear like portals to another world. Paintings like “Our Brief Passage Through Life (Nuestro breve paso por la vida)” share an affinity with the alchemical works of Spanish artist Remedios Varo, who portrayed more-than-human figures with odd proportions. 
Playing with scale and atypical pairings of objects and motifs is characteristic of Wong. Unlike the lifelike renditions she created as a sketch artist, these vivid paintings stray from any predetermined script and instead envision a world entirely her own.
If you’re in Chicago, see Journeys of Being through January 10. Keep up with Wong’s work on Instagram.
